text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency Andre Plankovich,
Prime Minister of the Republic of
Croatia. I request protocol to escort
his excellency and invite him to address
the assembly.
Good evening, Madame Chair,
excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We
come to this assembly from countries
that differ in size, population, and
power. Yet here, precisely because of
that, every country has its unique
experience to share, responsibilities to
assume, and a contribution to make.
Croatia brings the experience of a
nation that within one generation,
endured aggression and occupation,
defended its freedom, and rebuilt
itself. It joined UN, NATO, and the EU,
and developed a flourishing democracy
and a growing economy. Our path and our
transition were neither straight nor
easy, but we made it.
Over the past decade as prime minister,
I have seen Croatia translate those
experiences into progress at home and
more responsibility abroad. They have
reinforced three convictions that speak
directly to the theme of this session.
First, rules are our common compass.
Second, transformation
help us build resilience.
Third, trust is earned only through
delivery.
Ladies and gentlemen, we support
rule-based multilateralism as the
pinnacle of human cooperation.
Not because we are naive, but because we
have seen and experienced the
alternative. For smaller and
medium-sized states, international law
is not an abstraction. It is the line
between order and tyranny, between
sovereign equality and the rule of
force. the rule of force such as
witnessed by Croatia during the brutal
aggression and occupation of more than
one quarter of our territory in the '90s
in the war which claimed nearly 20,000
lives and after which more than three
decades later Croatia continues to
search for 1,725
missing persons. a poant example that
the consequences of war do not end when
the weapons fall silent. Instead, peace
requires courage, credible institutions,
and rules that apply equally to
everyone. Russia's ongoing war of
aggression against Ukraine is a direct
assault on those rules. Croatia will
continue to support Ukraine's
sovereignty, independence, and
territorial integrity and a
comprehensive, just and lasting peace
based on the UN charter. Peace cannot
reward conquest, and recovery cannot be
separated from justice.
The same compass must guide us in the
Middle East. Protection of civilians,
unhindered humanitarian access, respect
for international law, and a credible
political horizon are essential to
breaking the cycle of violence. Croatia
supports a negotiated two-state solution
in which Israelis and Palestinians will
live in peace and security. From Sudan
and Myanmar to the Sahel and the Great
Lakes region, civilians bear the highest
cost when rules are ignored and
diplomacy fails. And no crisis remains
local for long. War disrupts food and
energy supplies while insecurity
from the straight of Hormuz to the Black
Sea affects shipping prices and
livelihoods across continents.
This is why as a government we are
dealing with the consequences of energy
price pressures by passing degrees to
protect Croatian citizens and economy
from energy shocks created far away from
our shores. As distant as they may seem,
these shocks are real as they ripple
into domestic inflationary pressures
affecting everything from wages and
pensions to food prices and basic
services. This is why freedom of
navigation, maritime security, and the
strict implementation of the United
Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
matter to everyone. For us, freedom of
navigation and maritime security are
both a national interest and a global
responsibility.
Common rules do not hold us back. They
provide the stability and predictability
necessary for countries to advance their
ambitions.
The world is being transformed by
technology, climate change, demographic
pressures, illegal migration, and
geopolitical rivalry. Our responsibility
is to govern them so that change expands
human freedom and security. Instead of
weakening them, the United Nations must
begin with its own transformation.
Croatia supports a UN that is more
effective, accountable, and financially
sustainable, and stronger across all
three pillars: peace and security,
sustainable development, and of course,
human rights. Reform must also produce a
more representative and effective
security council. When the council is
blocked, the general assembly can and
must act, but it cannot replace the
council's primary responsibility under
the charter. This makes the selection of
the next secretary general all the more
relevant. I thank therefore Secretary
General Gutes for his work over the last
decade. The United Nations needs
leadership capable of bringing member
states together, defending the charter,
and turning reform into measurable
results. No country alone can
successfully respond to the global
transformations we witness today.
Artificial intelligence can accelerate
development, but its use must remain
consistent with legal frameworks, human
dignity, and democratic accountability.
Renewed nuclear rehetoric makes a firm
commitment to the treaty on the
non-prololiferation of nuclear weapons
more important than ever. Climate action
should be used to strengthen energy
security and social cohesion. Our
experience shows that the green
transition should not be ideological.
It can endure only when it is
technologically realistic, socially
fair, compatible with secure and
affordable energy, and supportive of
overall development. For Europe, which
imports most of the energy it consumes,
the case for producing more renewable
energy at home, now reaches far beyond
climate policy. It is a strategic
necessity. It strengthens Europe's
sovereignty and capacity to act, reduces
external dependence, creates economic
opportunity, and makes our societies
more resilient.
The same principle applies to illegal
migration, which has caused mistrust in
Europe and altered the political
landscape in many countries. This
situation is unacceptable and it cannot
continue. The rule of law must be upheld
and legal procedures must be followed.
Our primary responsibility is to our
citizens and it starts at our borders.
We are not allowing uncontrolled
migration and we are fighting the
criminal networks that facilitate it. As
an EU external border country, Croatia
carries an additional responsibility and
we will fulfill it with determination.
Transformation is equally important in
our own neighborhood. Southeast Europe
remains the unfinished part of the
European project. Croatia will continue
to support merit-based EU enlargement.
EU membership can turn borders of
division into lines of cooperation and
reforms on paper into stronger
institutions and better living
standards. But European transformation
requires honesty about the past.
Reconciliation becomes possible when
responsibility for the crimes of the
past is acknowledged and their
glorification rejected.
That standard allows no national
exceptions. That means respect for
victims and clear rejection of
historical revisionism, not the
glorification of war criminals. Ratcom
Ladic was a convicted war criminal
responsible for the Sbranita genocide,
the first genocide in Europe since the
Holocaust.
While his criminal record reached its
nefarious culmination in Sbranita, his
trail of war crimes stretches further
back to the shelling of Croatian cities,
the murder of civilians, the mining of
dams, and the destruction of cultural
heritage and industrial facilities. The
military and official honors accorded to
Madic in Serbia were an affront to his
victims and to the judgments of
international courts. The participation
of state representatives and the public
acclaim that accompanied the ceremony is
totally incompatible with the values of
a union Serbia seeks to join. The same
commitment to equality and reform should
guide Bosnian Herzgoina. As a signary to
the Dayton Peace Accords and a neighbor
and a friend of Bosnian Herzgoina,
Croatia is one of the strongest
advocates of its European future. The
Dayton Peace Accords ended the war and
established the constitutional framework
for Bosnian Herzgoina. one state, two
entities and three constituent peoples,
Croats, Bosnjaks and Serbs. That balance
is the foundation on which peace was
built. Yet the Cros of Bosnian Herziggo
are still being denied legitimate
representation,
including in the presidency of the
country. That is unjust, destabilizing,
and contrary to the spirit of Dayton.
The solution is neither division nor
domination. It is carefully designed
electoral reform that protects every
citizens while ensuring that a basic
principle of legitimate political
representation of the constituent
peoples is restored.
Croatia will not tire of explaining why
this reform is crucial for the entire
country to reach its full potential. And
we will not tire of opposing those
political forces whose short-sighted
pursuit of political gains jeopardizes
equality of constituent peoples and the
long-term prosperity. Our own history
confirms that transformation succeeds
when it is rooted in inclusion,
responsibility, and reform.
Over the past decade, Croatia has
doubled the size of its economy in
nominal terms while reducing its public
debt to GDP ratio by 30 percentage
points from its pandemic peak. Six
consecutive sovereign credit rating
upgrades have brought us into the A
category. We have tripled our defense
budget with approximately onethird of
that spending allocated to military
modernization.
In a change security environment, we are
strengthening our security and ensuring
we are better equipped to support
international stabilization missions
abroad. Reforms we are pursuing
domestically are increasing our overall
resilience and giving us increased
capacity to engage in a world which is
rapidly changing.
Ladies and gentlemen, the international
system stutters when the distance
between declaration and delivery becomes
too wide. Trust returns when cooperation
produces real measurable results. It
returns when a child is in school, a
community is protected from violence, a
mine is removed from a field, or food
reaches family. And it returns when
institutions prevent conflict before it
even begins. Last year alone, the
world's official development assistance
was reduced by almost 25%.
This drop is the largest annual
contraction on record for international
aid. Refusing to spiral into negative
trends, Croatia is contributing more,
not less. Between 2016 and 24, our
official development assistance
increased five-fold, while our
humanitarian assistance grew more than
21fold. With our UN partners, we are
translating our commitment and funds
into action. We support girls education
in Kenya, provide humanitarians
assistance in Gaza, and assist Syrian
refugee children. We also advine advance
mine action in Ukraine drawing on
Croatia's own post-war experience and
protect women and girls from digital
violence. This practical, inclusive and
human- centered approach is also what
Croatia brings to Echosok. If elected to
the presidency of Echos for the 2728
cycle, Croatia will work to strengthen
coordination and accountability.
As 2030 approaches, accelerating
implementation of the sustainable goals
continues to be a central priority.
Croatia persistently ranks among the
world's 15 highest performing countries
in implementing the sustainable
development goals. Our experience is not
a universal prescription but evidence
that national reform and international
responsibility can and do advance
together. It is this credibility that is
in the foundation of trust in
multilateralism that we wish to see
rebuilt. Credibility which is strongest
when every country regardless of its
size, wealth or power has a meaningful
voice. The answer is therefore not less
multilateralism that delivers. It is
multilateralism that must deliver. It is
this approach that Croatia would bring
to the security council if elected to
serve in 203031.
Excellencies, Croatia's modern journey
began in war, but war did not define its
destination. Our experience has shaped
the way we understand international
cooperation and the responsibilities
that come with it. Rules gave us a
compass when force sought to erase our
borders. Reform gave us a bridge from
vulnerability to resilience and from
postwar recovery to membership in the
EU, the Euro area and Shenhen. delivery
turned those ambitions into
institutions, security and better lives
for our citizens and gave us the
capacity to contribute beyond our
borders. That is the experience Croatia
brings to the United Nations. Not a
claim to perfection, but the perspective
of a country that has traveled the
difficult road and learned from it. The
United Nations remains indispensable
because no country can navigate today's
storms alone.
Let us therefore rebuild trust by
defending our common compass and
managing change so that it strengthens
human dignity. Let us ensure that our
commitment reach the people for whom
they were made. Thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the prime minister of the Republic
of Croatia.
